courses.title: Body-Mind Education
courses.brief_description: Movement, play, reflection, and connection
courses.description: BODY-MIND EDUCATION (One Semester) All 9th-graders participate in Body-Mind Education (BME). BME offers students a holistic and nurturing experience as they transition into high school, providing a safe and supportive learning environment where students feel seen, valued, and appreciated. Prioritizing movement, play, reflection, and connection, BME offers relevant, meaningful, and engaging learning experiences that balance individual growth and community collaboration. All BME instructors emphasize bodily autonomy and self-care, providing students with a variety of options for meeting challenges while honoring their own needs and boundaries. HEALTH & WELLNESS (One Quarter) The Health & Wellness section of the Body-Mind Education curriculum serves as a forum for students to explore meaningful teen health topics in a safe and structured environment. Students will explore personal values, engage in respectful dialogue, and develop critical thinking skills as they delve more deeply into the complex terrain of adolescence. We’ll consider a variety of topics throughout the course, including mental health awareness and stress skills, time management and study habits, sleep and nutrition, adolescent brain development, substance education, and healthy peer relationships. The curriculum incorporates games, journaling, discussion, media, surveys, and collaborative creative projects. MOVEMENT (One Quarter) The Movement Curriculum is a dynamic program designed to inspire students to gain a comprehensive understanding of their bodies while empowering them physically, mentally, and emotionally. This innovative course offers a diverse range of activities, exercises, and collaborative games integrated through rock climbing and yoga, allowing students to excel regardless of their initial fitness level. Students will build foundational physical abilities such as strength, flexibility, isometric endurance, balance, and proprioception while developing strategies such as breath control and meditation that will support them throughout their high school journey, Additionally, the course is designed to encourage the collaborative enjoyment of movement, creating a supportive environment that fosters both individual growth and community. Semester course offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027.

courses.title: Sacred Mountains: Rock Climbing and Environmental Justice PPP
courses.brief_description: Climbing, ecology, and environmental justice
courses.description: This UC “G” elective course explores the meeting point of body, nature, and justice through rock climbing, eco-somatic inquiry, and community engagement across the San Francisco Bay Area. Students will develop daily practices to reconnect with the natural world—even within our urban landscape—and learn how presence, movement, and awareness can deepen our sense of belonging to the Earth. Through climbing, field experiences, and collaboration with local organizations, we will explore climate action and environmental justice as living, embodied practices rooted in relationship, reciprocity, and care. No prior climbing experience or equipment is required. Prerequisites: One semester of BME This course is offered in both Fall 2025 and Spring 2026 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: Soph Health: Human Sexuality
courses.brief_description: Human sexuality, identity, and healthy relationships
courses.description: (One semester) The Body-Mind Education department’s semester-long course for 10th-graders, “Soph Health: Human Sexuality,” offers an inclusive and well-structured space for students to explore the complex realm of sexuality, traversing culture, identity, intersectionality, values, relationships, pornography literacy, sexual health, safer sex, pleasure, and consent, among other topics. Drawing from readings, media, discussion, games, role-playing, films, surveys, creative projects, and journals, students will engage in open and respectful dialogue, clarify personal values, and critically confront the wider cultures that surround, inform, and  shape their lives. Prerequisite: One semester of Body-Mind Education. Semester course offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027

courses.title: Yoga For Change: Breathe, Move, & Inspire PPP
courses.brief_description: Yoga, mindfulness, fitness, and leadership
courses.description: Ready to deepen your yoga practice while making a difference? In this course, you'll dive into yoga as a powerful tool for self-care, physical fitness, and mindfulness; helping you find balance and focus in your daily life. But it doesn’t stop there. You’ll also get the chance to inspire younger kids by teaching them yoga in schools where PE and recess programs have been cut. This is your chance to share what you learn, build leadership skills, and help others discover the benefits of yoga. If you’re passionate about growing your practice and supporting others, this PPP course is for you!  Semester course offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027.

courses.title: Zen in the Bay: A Holistic Exploration of Buddhist Meditation & Practice
courses.brief_description: Zen, mindfulness, and personal exploration
courses.description: This UC “G” elective course invites students into a meaningful exploration of Zen Buddhism and mindfulness practice through classroom learning and immersive experiences around the San Francisco Bay Area. We will explore meditation, neuroscience, ethics, art, and social engagement as ways of understanding and cultivating awareness in daily life. Students will learn and practice simple forms of meditation, reflect through journaling and creative projects, engage in small group discussions, and participate in field trips to local Buddhist centers and natural spaces. The course emphasizes balance, curiosity, and personal exploration over academic rigor—offering space to slow down, breathe, and experience what it means to live with greater clarity and compassion. Prerequisites: One semester of BME. This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved,

courses.title: Creative Writing: Crafting Stories for Children and Young Adults PPP
courses.brief_description: Writing diverse, impactful children's and YA literature
courses.description: Children's and young adult literature has the power to shape how young readers see themselves and the world around them. In this course, students will learn the craft of writing stories for children and teens—stories that matter, stories that fill gaps in representation, stories that respond to the cultural moment we're living in. Through hands-on writing exercises, close study of mentor texts, and workshop sessions, students will explore techniques for creating compelling characters, vivid worlds, authentic dialogue, and narratives that resonate with young readers. Students will experiment with multiple forms—from picture books to middle grade to young adult fiction—and develop their unique voices as storytellers. Throughout the course, students will ask: What is this story for? What new perspective does it offer? How might it shift, expand, or challenge a young reader's understanding of themselves, others, and what's possible? At the heart of this course is the belief that a supportive creative community can inspire writers to take risks, experiment boldly, and craft stories that young readers need. Public Purpose Program: Students will partner with an organization promoting LGBTQ+ literature and combating book censorship (such as Books Not Bans or Drag Story Hour) to support their missions through fundraising, digital content creation, and other community outreach activities. Prerequisites: English 1 This UC approved course is offered in Spring 2027 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: English 1
courses.brief_description: The study of literature and writing
courses.description: The English 1 curriculum prepares students for the study of literature and writing at LWHS. Students practice the skills of careful reading, listening, and speaking as they encounter literature in a variety of genres. Students are also introduced to and practice the foundations of analytical writing—composing thesis statements, embedding textual evidence, and analyzing text. Students examine their own values and perspectives as they read and write. In particular, they are asked to consider the ways in which expectations for reading and writing change in high school. Learning collaboratively is also a significant focus of the class as students work in groups to construct theories, explore evidence, and ask questions. Prerequisite: None This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.

courses.title: English 2
courses.brief_description: Fiction, drama, and poetry
courses.description: The English 2 curriculum focuses on world literature. Students read core texts comprising fiction, drama, and poetry. Essential questions guide their critical thinking, while student-led discussions allow for literary exploration from a variety of perspectives. Students learn to closely read and make thoughtful annotations, in addition to frequently writing analytical and creative responses to literature. With an emphasis on revision over time, student writing culminates in a final portfolio that showcases growth and mastery. Prerequisite: English 1 This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors English 3
courses.brief_description: Careful reading and critical analysis of literature
courses.description: The Honors English 3 curriculum focuses on reading and writing about literature from the United States. As students engage in careful reading and critical analysis, the course develops awareness about how language and story construct identity, both individual and communal. In particular, students advance their close reading, specifically their understanding of detail, diction, imagery, syntax, and structure. Students write in a variety of genres and continue to develop strategies for crafting sophisticated arguments supported by precise textual evidence and analysis. A focus on stylistic and grammatical clarity becomes increasingly significant in writing instruction. Both group activities and whole class discussions are central to the study of the course texts. Collaborative projects and presentations encourage students to take on greater intellectual leadership in the classroom. Prerequisite: English 2 This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors English 4: (En)gendered Violence
courses.brief_description: US literature and philosophy about gendered forms of violence
courses.description: In this course, we will read US literature and philosophy (drawing from feminist theory and masculinity studies) about gendered forms of violence. We’ll read and discuss texts about domestic violence and rape; asking how US institutions, history, and belief systems contribute to those violent acts. We will also discuss texts that illustrate ways to heal and form healthy, supportive relationships. Texts include Anna Quindlen’s Black and Blue, Sandra Cisnero’s “Woman Hollering Creek,” and Alice Walker’s The Color Purple. Prerequisite: Honors English 3 This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors English 4: Black Joy: Visions of Power, Resistance & Hope in African American Literature
courses.brief_description: African American literature: identity, power, change
courses.description: Throughout its history, African American literature has always been a declaration of selfhood, an exercise of power, and a vision of what is possible. This course offers a peek into the breadth and depth of that African American literary tradition, tracing its evolution across genres and movements. Students will read and analyze a diverse range of texts — including poetry, fiction, essays, and narrative — engaging with writers whose work celebrates the complexity and vitality of Black experience in America. Through close reading, discussion, and analysis, students will explore how African American writers have claimed and defined identity on their own terms, wielded language as power while insisting on the beauty, and humanity of blackness in America. Transformation has always been central to the works of Black writers: how does art rooted in lived experience become a call to action? How do writers convert passion into collective power and visions of a liberated future? We will explore how resistance, and creative spirit recur and evolve throughout the works of Black American Artist. By the end of the course, students will have developed both a broad literary map of the African American tradition and the critical tools to engage it — not only as scholars, but as readers moved by its beauty, its boldness, and its enduring belief in the possibility of change. Texts may include works by artist such Langston Hughes, Gwendolyn Brooks, Sonia Sanchez, Nikki Giovanni, Amanda Gorman, Zora Neale Hurston, Toni Morrison, Octavia Butler, Colson Whitehead, James Baldwin, Audre Lorde, bell hooks, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Barry Jenkins, Ryan Coogler, Ava DuVernay, Nina Simone, Gil Scott-Heron Public Enemy, Kendrick Lamar and Beyoncé  Prerequisite: Honors English 3 This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors English 4: Carceral Culture: Stories, Histories, Alternatives PPP
courses.brief_description: Mass incarceration, race, narratives, justice
courses.description: Beyond TV shows like Law and Order or COPS, what are the stories that shape your understanding of the current system of mass incarceration in the United States? How do these stories impact your perception of people labelled “criminal” or “felon”? Michelle Alexander argues that with labels like these “we have not ended racial caste in America; we have merely redesigned it.” Angela Y. Davis goes further and argues that “[h]omelessness, unemployment, drug addiction, mental illness, and illiteracy are only a few of the problems that disappear from public view when the human beings contending with them are relegated to cages.”  This PPP seminar will explore the American system of mass criminalization from the inside out.  We’ll confront some obvious questions like why does the American system of punishment disproportionately target people of color? We’ll examine the role and power of language in shaping who gets systematically targeted? And we’ll explore alternatives to the current practice of locking people up. We will center the voices and experiences of those directly impacted by carceral culture through podcasts and first-person narratives. Throughout, we will frame our work through an antiracist lens to affirm the dignity and humanity of all people, embrace historical truths (including the untold truths), and develop a critical consciousness around how dominant narratives dominate and perpetuate marginalization* *Adapted from The Center for AntiRacist Education.  Participation in PPP days is a requirement to pass the class. Prerequisite: Honors English 3 This UC approved course is offered in Spring 2027 and fulfills the PPP requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: Honors English 4: Children vs. Monsters PPP
courses.brief_description: Monsters, queerness, censorship, childhood, power
courses.description: Monsters in literature have always marked boundaries: what's acceptable, what's dangerous, what threatens social order. They are frequently queer-coded figures who transgress norms and inhabit liminal spaces. Book banning operates by the same logic, marking certain stories—especially queer stories, stories of resistance—as threats to childhood "innocence" that must be kept out of children's hands. In this seminar, students will read children's and young adult literature through rigorous theoretical frameworks including Monster Theory, Childhood Studies, Liminality, Queer Theory, Intersectionality, and Feminist Studies. Students will examine how monsters function in stories, how certain books are themselves "monstered" through censorship, and how we celebrate children fighting monsters in fiction while real children face harm that goes unaddressed. Through close reading and theoretical analysis, students will explore what children's literature reveals about power, vulnerability, and the systems that shape childhood. Public Purpose Program: Students will partner with an organization promoting LGBTQ+ literature and combating book censorship (such as Books Not Bans or Drag Story Hour) to support their missions through fundraising, digital content creation, and other community outreach activities. Prerequisite: Honors English 3 This UC approved course is offered in Fall 2026 and fulfills the PPP requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: Honors English 4: Contagion and Regeneration: What Plagues Teach Us About Ourselves
courses.brief_description: Midwives, zombies, vampires, and beyond
courses.description: For centuries, plagues and epidemics have devastated human populations across the globe. As Albert Camus observed, such crises expose the underlying fissures within society. In moments of global health catastrophe, the social pathologies of capitalism and xenophobia can prove as lethal as the contagions themselves. Yet disaster also opens spaces for transformation. How do large-scale outbreaks reveal systemic injustices, and how might these moments of rupture offer opportunities to disrupt established power structures, dominant narratives, physical spaces and patterns of marginalization? During this course, together we will examine the ways authors use large scale disease outbreaks as a framework for cultural, political, and social critique. Reading texts that reflect the beliefs of Puritan England, the philosophy of the Absurd, and the concept of Ontological Expansiveness, students will explore how representations of plague challenge systems of class, capitalism, heteronormativity, and xenophobia and open up the spaces to reimagine alternative ways to live. Texts include: The Year of Wonders by Geraldine Brooks, The Plague by Albert Camus, Feral City: On Finding Liberation in Lockdown New York by Jeremiah Moss as well as additional supplementary texts and essays. Prerequisite: Honors English 3 This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Frosh Ethnic Studies
courses.brief_description: Critical Ethnic Studies perspectives
courses.description: Ethnic Studies is an interdisciplinary field of study that encompasses many subject areas including history, literature, economics, sociology, anthropology, and political science. It emerged to both address content considered missing from traditional curriculum and to encourage critical engagement.  As a field, Ethnic Studies seeks to empower all students to engage socially and politically and to think critically about the world around them. It is important for Ethnic Studies courses to document the experiences of People of Color in order for students to construct counter-narratives and develop a more complex understanding of the human experience. Through these studies, students should develop respect for cultural diversity and see the advantages of inclusion.  Because of the interdisciplinary nature of this field, Ethnic Studies courses may take several forms. However, central to any Ethnic Studies course is the historic struggle of communities of color, taking into account the intersectionality of identity (gender, class, sexuality, among others), to challenge racism, discrimination, and oppression and interrogate the systems that continue to perpetuate inequality. This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for freshmen. It is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors United States History
courses.brief_description: The United States from its origins to the present
courses.description: As a survey of United States history, this required 11th grade course offers students a study of the social, political, economic, and cultural developments and patterns that have formed the United States from its origins to the present. Our course’s guiding questions include: How has resistance to injustice shaped the nation? How do different groups understand injustice differently? What is the changing role of government in individuals’ lives? How are historical narratives created? How does historical narrative impact the actual unfolding of history? The assignments and activities focus on research, analysis, discussion, writing, presentation, and collaboration. We approach with the perspective that history shapes the way we understand ourselves, our communities, our nation, and our role in the world. Prerequisite: Modern World History This yearlong course is UC approved.

courses.title: Modern World History
courses.brief_description: Social, political, and economic historical developments from the early modern period through the Cold War
courses.description: The sophomore World History course highlights broad social, political, and economic historical developments from the early modern period through the Cold War. We will explore why global power structures have changed and what their impacts have been on modern global issues and current events. We also will examine systems of power, focusing on the ways they shaped interactions between peoples around the world. We will focus on major global developments including how the present has been shaped by the great global convergence, Atlantic revolutions, industrialization, imperialism, resistance movements and global conflicts. Students will learn and practice historical skills including research, source analysis, discussion, writing, presentation, and collaboration. Prerequisite: None This yearlong course is UC approved.

courses.title: Modern World History Seminar: A Collision of Cultures: Identity in Latin America
courses.brief_description: Identity in Modern Latin America
courses.description: Latin America has a deep impact on our culture—the way we speak, the way we dress, what we eat, and of course how we view some of the most pressing political issues of the day.  Yet for some reason, Americans are particularly ignorant about the historical narrative of the myriad peoples , cultures, and nations that exist to our South. With this in mind, this course examines the ethnic, racial, gender, economic, and cultural diversity of Latin America. It considers how cultural encounters between and among diverse identities during the course of the region’s history have manifested themselves in the modern popular culture, politics and economics of the region. Students will examine the impact of immigration, slavery, and genocide on the emergence of geographic, ethnic, and cultural enclaves, and the constant re-formulation of identities in Latin America. It will also discuss and complicate the term Latino (or “Latinx”) and what it means, both in the US and beyond. Students in the course should come away with an understanding of both the nature and importance of Latino as an identity, and also of the various challenges inherent in the creation of the category. Oh, and you’ll also hear a lot of great music! This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Modern World History Seminar: Foodways: Food & Community in World History
courses.brief_description: Peoples' culture and identity through food
courses.description: Human history is mirrored in the diverse ways that our ancestors learned to feed themselves, the culinary practices they developed and how they are tied to enduring stories of culture and identity, especially after the agricultural revolution.  This course asks students to consider the historical dynamics that shaped how different peoples approached food and what that reveals about their larger social, spiritual, economic and political values.  We will better understand the historical spread of foodways and the challenges created by industrialized food systems today through historical inquiry, storytelling, one local field trip, self-directed cooking at home and by celebrating the art of eating. Prerequisite: Honors U.S. History This course is offered in Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Modern World History Seminar: Indigenous Peoples & Voices in the Present
courses.brief_description: The historical and contemporary experiences of Indigenous groups in the Americas
courses.description: Indigenous peoples were the original inhabitants of the Western Hemisphere and despite facing centuries of genocide and erasure, their stories, legacies and descendents are still here because of Native survivance. This Indigenous Studies course asks students to consider the historical and contemporary experiences of first nations in the Americas by centering their stories and voices to highlight their histories, communal values and resilience. Our historical understanding will be enriched through mixed media, literature, films, the work of indigenous activists, a field trip and ceremonies. Prerequisite: Honors U.S. History This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: U.S. History Seminar: The U.S. and the Middle East
courses.brief_description: An exploration of the relationship between the US and the Middle East
courses.description: The Middle East has long held a place of importance in the cultural imagination of Americans, and more recently has played an outsized role in the political and economic narrative of American history.  This course examines the history and complexities of US-Middle Eastern relations through an exploration of the issues that have defined this relationship.  Oil, religion, imperialism, the Arab-Israeli Conflict, the Cold War, “terrorism,” Islamophobia, and more recently, the rise of ISIS, refugee crises, the Arab Spring, and US-Iranian tensions are among the many issues that students in this course will explore.  Students in the course will undertake both original research projects and more action-oriented work that seeks to illuminate the structures of power and ideologies that have underpinned US-Middle Eastern Relations.   Prerequisite: Honors U.S. History This course is offered in Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: US History Seminar: Asian American Activism
courses.brief_description: Asian American activism: history, identity, solidarity
courses.description: Is there a unifying characteristic of Asian American activism, and if so, how can it guide us today? By studying the visions, methods, and challenges of a range of examples of Asian American activism across time and place, we will respond to those questions and more. At a time of emphasis on the wide range of experiences and histories of specific Asian American communities, we investigate and evaluate the current need for and significance of the term Asian American. By engaging closely with how Asian American activists have thought of themselves and their commitments to global visions toward liberation, we make room to consider the relationships between activism and healing and between lineage and love. We will support the ongoing work of Asian American activists and will share dimensions of our learning with the LWHS community, ultimately making solidarity not only an aspiration but a felt, immediate reality.  Prerequisite: Honors U.S. History This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: US History Seminar: Bay Area History PPP
courses.brief_description: Bay Area history, identity, and citizenship
courses.description: In this course, we will investigate the history of the Bay Area through four historical lenses: environmental history, labor history, immigration history, and political history. With each of these lenses, we will examine major moments in the region’s history to understand how the Bay Area became the dynamic, radical hub of technological and political progress that it is today. Additionally, this will be a PPP course, so within each unit, we will guide our learning with essential questions about our present day impact and engagement in the region. Ultimately, these investigations will help us get closer to an answer for a perennially important question—what does it mean to be a citizen of the Bay Area? The course will feature reading, writing, creative work, field trips, service learning, and community engagement. This UC approved course is offered in Spring 2027 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: US History Seminar: Civic Power PPP
courses.brief_description: Civic engagement, power, and social change
courses.description: Civic Power explores how people and institutions work to create change in their communities. Through research and discussion, we will investigate how power operates in democratic systems and where opportunities for civic engagement exist. We will examine how federal, state, and local governments shape policies to address issues from housing to education, considering where conflicts emerge, and how power structures and decision-making happen. We will then explore how nonprofits, advocacy groups, and grassroots organizations work alongside—or sometimes in place of—government to address community needs. We will also examine the role of art, music, and media in protest movements, exploring how creative expression has been used to challenge injustice and inspire social change. As part of the PPP component, we will engage with local community organizations, help organize a community resource fair, and ultimately collaborate to help others understand the power individuals have to create change. This UC approved course is offered in Spring 2027 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: US History Seminar: Ethnic Studies Seminar—School: Purpose and Possibility PPP
courses.brief_description: Education, democracy, and Ethnic Studies history
courses.description: What did W.E.B. Du Bois mean in 1923 when he said that “the public school is the only real foundation for democracy,” and what do we make of that vision today? We will trace various meanings of education and schooling throughout United States history, and we will follow our own honest inquiries about the lives and hopes of students and teachers. As we begin Ethnic Studies for ninth graders here at LWHS, we additionally will use this course as an opportunity simultaneously to engage more thoroughly with the history of the Third World Liberation Front (TWLF) at San Francisco State and also to surface histories of LWHS that, together, can move us toward what is possible, toward what more fully realizes our own public purpose.  This UC approved course is offered in Spring 2027 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: Juniors and seniors (sophomores only with significant exception) may participate in semester-long independent studies to investigate a topic in a discipline not offered at LWHS (e.g. economics) or a topic not covered in-depth in the curriculum (e.g. Native American history). Students must apply for an independent study by submitting a detailed proposal that includes—a pointed question that the student will investigate, a syllabus detailing what materials the student will explore, and a description of the proposed final product. While a faculty member must supervise an independent study, the work of planning and executing the independent study is the responsibility of the student. (new faculty may not sponsor in their first year) Aside from shops-based independent studies that may require supervision, students should expect to check in with their supervising teacher roughly once a rotation. In short, independent studies should be independent. The supervising teacher, the appropriate Department Chair, and the Dean of Teaching and Learning must review and sign the proposal. A student may conduct only one Independent Study in an academic year, either fall or spring semester, and it does not count as one of the six required courses. All Independent Studies are graded pass/fail. Teachers may supervise only one independent study per academic year.  This course is offered in both Fall 2024 and Spring 2025.

courses.title: Independent Study PPP
courses.description: Juniors and seniors (sophomores only with significant exception) may participate in semester-long independent studies to investigate a topic in a discipline not offered at LWHS (e.g. economics) or a topic not covered in-depth in the curriculum (e.g. Native American history). Students must apply for an independent study by submitting a detailed proposal that includes—a pointed question that the student will investigate, a syllabus detailing what materials the student will explore, and a description of the proposed final product. A PPP Independent Study also requires a summary of the student’s public purpose/community partnership commitment. While a faculty-staff member must supervise an independent study, the work of planning and executing the independent study is the responsibility of the student. (new faculty-staff may not sponsor in their first year).  The supervising teacher, the appropriate Department Chair,  the Dean of Teaching and Learning and the Director of the Public Purpose Program must review and sign the proposal. A student may conduct only one PPP Independent Study in an academic year, either fall or spring semester, and it does not count as one of the six required courses. All PPP Independent Studies are graded pass/fail. Teachers may supervise only one PPP independent study per academic year.  This course is offered in both Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: Accelerated Algebra 2
courses.brief_description: A faster pace and a more theoretical approach to learning algebra
courses.description: Accelerated Algebra 2 is an intermediate algebra course intended for those who can benefit from a faster pace and a more theoretical approach to learning algebra. In addition to material covered in Algebra 2, it includes a more thorough treatment of complex numbers and a more in-depth study of polynomials, rational, exponential, and logarithmic functions. An enrichment unit on topics such as linear algebra and vectors will also be included if time allows.  The course encourages a variety of approaches to problem solving using mathematical models, with extensive use of graphical methods. A strong foundation in algebraic/symbolic manipulation is needed. Students are expected to solve skill-based problems as well as non-routine problems that require creative problem solving and experimentation.  Students who successfully complete this course move on to Precalculus or Precalculus Honors with department recommendation. Prerequisites: Inductive or Deductive Geometry and department recommendation This course is offered yearlong and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Inductive or Deductive Geometry and department recommendation

courses.title: Algebra 1
courses.brief_description: A review of the number system, fractions, and percents, as well as an introduction to mathematical symbols and operations
courses.description: This course deepens and extends students’ understanding of elementary algebra, building the foundational tools needed for success in subsequent math courses. It begins with a review of the number system, fractions, and percents, along with an introduction to mathematical symbols and operations. From there, students explore ratios; simplification and factoring of variable expressions; solutions to linear equations, inequalities, and systems; graphing linear equations and inequalities in two variables; and modeling real-world situations. Throughout the course, students engage with concepts through numeric, symbolic, verbal, and visual representations. Emphasis is placed on mathematical thinking practices that promote reasoning and conceptual understanding, rather than rote memorization of algorithms, rules and formulas. Students who successfully complete this course move on to Inductive Geometry or Deductive Geometry with department recommendation. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.

courses.title: Algebra 2
courses.brief_description: Expands understanding of topics explored in Algebra 1 and Geometry
courses.description: Algebra 2 deepens and expands understanding of topics explored in Algebra 1 and Geometry, and introduces advanced topics that include: function notation, function transformations, arithmetic and geometric sequences, inverse functions, and exponential and logarithmic functions. A variety of approaches to problem-solving is encouraged with an emphasis on mathematical thinking practices. The course is centered on collaborative student exploration, discovery, and gradual development of understanding, using materials written specifically for this class. Students who successfully complete this course move on to Precalculus or Statistics. Prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Inductive or Deductive Geometry This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Inductive or Deductive Geometry

courses.title: Calculus
courses.brief_description: The fundamental concepts and techniques of differential and integral calculus
courses.description: This course explores the fundamental concepts and techniques of differential and integral calculus—the mathematics of change.  This course will follow a traditional sequence of topics, starting in the fall with limits and then studying the derivative and applications of the derivative.  The spring is a complete examination and analysis of the integral, starting with investigations using motion as a framework. The crux of the spring semester will be formalizing the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and then applying it in different contexts, such as area and volume. One  cornerstone of this course is learning through extensive “lab” investigations. Prerequisites: Precalculus with a second semester grade of at least B-, strong algebraic preparation, and department recommendation. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Precalculus with a second semester grade of at least B-, strong algebraic preparation, and department recommendation.

courses.title: Deductive Geometry
courses.brief_description: Deductive approach and formal study of geometric concepts pioneered by Euclid
courses.description: This course is a traditional geometry course that follows the deductive approach and formal study of geometric concepts pioneered by Euclid. Students begin with an introduction to logic and proceed to prove many of the classical theorems of Euclidean geometry and apply these ideas to challenging problems. Additional topics include quadratic expressions and equations, systems of linear equations, and right triangle trigonometry. Students will engage in solving interesting and meaningful problems while practicing school-wide habits of mind and mathematical thinking practices. Prerequisites: Algebra 1 at LWHS with department recommendation, or department recommendation (incoming 9th graders). This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 at LWHS with department recommendation, or department recommendation (incoming 9th graders).

courses.title: Honors Calculus
courses.brief_description: The foundational concepts of Calculus and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and series
courses.description: The course is structured around big ideas corresponding to the foundational concepts of Calculus: limits, derivatives, integrals and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and series. Students will use Mathematical Practices and Habits of Mind in their study to establish mathematical lines of reasoning and to apply mathematical concepts and tools to solve problems. These Mathematical Practices include reasoning with definitions and theorems, connecting concepts, implementing algebraic/computational processes, connecting multiple representations, building notational fluency, and strengthening mathematical discourse. Precalculus or Precalculus Honors, and department recommendation. Students coming from Precalculus will need to do additional study during the preceding summer and take a LWHS placement exam to determine final placement. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors Multivariable Calculus
courses.brief_description: Vector and Multivariable Calculus
courses.description: This course covers vector and multivariable calculus. Topics include vectors and vector-valued functions, curves and surfaces in space, partial derivatives and gradients, multiple integration, and line and surface integrals. Throughout the course, students will use Mathematical Practices and Habits of Mind to establish mathematical lines of reasoning and to apply mathematical concepts and tools to solve problems. These Mathematical Practices include reasoning with definitions and theorems, connecting concepts, implementing algebraic/computational processes, connecting multiple representations, building notational fluency, and strengthening mathematical discourse. Prerequisites: Calculus (regular or honors) and department recommendation. Students coming from Calculus will need to do additional study during the preceding summer and take an LWHS placement exam to determine final placement. This course is offered yearlong and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Calculus (regular or honors) and department recommendation. Students coming from Calculus will need to do additional study during the preceding summer and take an LWHS placement exam to determine final placement.

courses.title: Honors Precalculus
courses.brief_description: Trigonometry, exponential and logarithmic functions, polar coordinates, parametric equations, and beyond
courses.description: Honors Precalculus explores functions and relations in greater depth. This includes the study of trigonometry, exponential and logarithmic functions, polar coordinates, parametric equations, and complex numbers. Students are expected to regularly work on non-routine problems by applying and building upon the content taught in previous math courses. Continuous review and problem solving are at the heart of the course, helping students to independently discover connections between new and old concepts.  Precalculus Honors also places emphasis on the modeling process in order to prompt students to make connections between theoretical mathematics and real world applications.  Prerequisites: Algebra 2 (regular or accelerated) and department recommendation. Students coming from Algebra 2 will need to do additional study during the preceding summer and take an LWHS placement exam to determine final placement. This course is offered yearlong and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 2 (regular or accelerated) and department recommendation. Students coming from Algebra 2 will need to do additional study during the preceding summer and take an LWHS placement exam to determine final placement.

courses.title: Honors Statistics and Data Science PPP
courses.brief_description: Draw meaningful conclusions from data
courses.description: This course develops students into ethical and competent consumers and producers of statistics by teaching them to draw meaningful conclusions from data. The first semester focuses on descriptive statistics and the question, What stories do the data tell? Students analyze one- and two-variable data using graphical and numerical methods, supported by technology and data science tools. The second semester shifts to inferential statistics, guided by the questions, Should I be surprised? and Is the difference meaningful? Topics include probability, random variables, and statistical significance testing. A Public Purpose Program project is integrated throughout the course. Prerequisites: Algebra 2 and department recommendation. This yearlong course fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors. It is a UC approved course.

courses.title: Acting
courses.brief_description: Theatre games, script and character analysis, and devised theatre
courses.description: Acting, an enjoyable and accessible art form, is a foundational drama course that empowers students to express themselves through theatrical performance. The course equips students with core competencies in voice, movement, and character analysis, fostering their imagination and enabling them to perform with clarity and emotional depth. Through scene study and improvisation, students engage in both group and solo acting projects, enhancing their craft. The course objectives are twofold: to foster student engagement in creative play and imagination, and to provide individualized actor coaching. Additionally, students develop valuable life skills such as public speaking, risk-taking, and problem-solving. In the second semester, students delve into in-depth scenework, docudrama, devised theatre, and Theatre Activism, further enriching their acting experience. Prerequisite: None. Open to all grades. This course is offered yearlong and is UC approved.

courses.title: Advanced Creative Projects in Music Production
courses.brief_description: Music production, sound design and composition
courses.description: This course builds upon the skills learned in Creative Projects in Music Production.  Students will work with Logic Pro and advanced plug-ins to create music tracks using MIDI, samples, and recorded audio.  Guest speakers will present on related topics in music production, sound design and composition. Students will design and execute their own digital music projects.  Prerequisite: Creative Projects in Music Production This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Advanced Jazz & Contemporary Music Ensemble PPP
courses.brief_description: Advanced ensemble performance, leadership, and musicianship
courses.description: The Advanced Jazz & Contemporary Music Ensemble is the upper level contemporary music course at LWHS. Geared toward musicians in grades 11–12, students are required to possess advanced proficiency of their instruments and have a strong foundation in music fundamentals. Students must demonstrate self discipline and maturity to participate in and lead project-based activities, public service projects, peer tutoring, and public speaking. Students in the course will work in both large and small ensemble configurations to develop ensemble and improvisational technique. The course emphasizes developing repertoire for concert and community service performances. Additionally students will cultivate outreach opportunities, and mentor beginning musicians from within and/or beyond the school. Students will hone their musicianship and performance experience through course rehearsals and participation in appropriate concerts and festivals. Applicable music theory and analysis is also a component of the course. Students will be assigned to varying sized combos to study and prepare a variety of stylistically appropriate music for public performance. Prerequisite: Three years of playing experience. One year in another LWHS ensemble (or the equivalent) and a successful placement audition/interview. Admission in one academic year does not guarantee placement in subsequent years. Participation in both the Fall and Spring Jazz Concerts and corresponding tech week rehearsals are mandatory for the course.  This yearlong course is UC approved and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.
courses.prerequisites: Three years of playing experience. One year in another LWHS ensemble (or the equivalent) and a successful placement audition/interview. Admission in one academic year does not guarantee placement in subsequent years.

courses.title: Advanced Stagecraft PPP
courses.brief_description: Design scenery, lights, sound, and costumes for school productions and partner organizations
courses.description: This class is for students who want to increase their skills in stagecraft and production work and continue their involvement in LWHS performances. Advanced Stagecraft students will lead the design of scenery, lights, sound, or costumes for department productions. This class is offered simultaneously with Stagecraft. Advanced Stagecraft students will be expected to take on leadership roles in the class, guiding building projects and stage crews. Students will work closely with our outside partner organizations designing and building projects for their performances. Prerequisite: Stagecraft This semester course is offered both in Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors. It is a UC approved course.

courses.title: Chamber Orchestra PPP
courses.brief_description: Intermediate-to-advanced orchestra, technique, and outreach
courses.description: Chamber Orchestra is for intermediate to advanced string, woodwind, brass, piano, and percussion instrumentalists. Repertoire is drawn from orchestral and chamber music literature of the western classical tradition, orchestral pops, as well as through creative explorations and adaptations of new music. Additionally, the ensemble engages guest composers to create works for the course. Emphasis is on ensemble playing, refining instrumental technique, and building musicianship. Listening activities and applicable music theory assignments are included in the coursework. Students are expected to practice at home and are encouraged to study their instruments privately when possible. The department owns many school instruments that are available for student use. Students will fulfill their PPP requirement through the planning and implementation of community outreach performances, exploring arts advocacy, arts equity, and peer mentoring. Prerequisite: One year of ensemble experience, intermediate music reading proficiency, and a successful placement audition. Participation in one academic year does not guarantee placement in subsequent years. Participation in both the Fall and Spring Chamber Orchestra Concerts and corresponding tech week rehearsals is mandatory for this course.  This yearlong course is UC approved and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.
courses.prerequisites: One year of ensemble experience, intermediate music reading proficiency, and a successful placement audition. Participation in one academic year does not guarantee placement in subsequent years.

courses.title: Creative Projects in Music Production
courses.brief_description: The fundamentals of music technology
courses.description: This course offers the perfect approach for students with a passion for music outside of traditional school music offerings. It will survey the fundamentals of music technology, including multitrack music production using a digital audio workstation (DAW), MIDI, recording, and basic principles of sound and digital audio technology.  Introductory topics include studio setup, how to write and record tracks for instruments using a MIDI sequencer, basic music editing and arrangement using music sequencing software, effects and plugins, and how to record live sounds. Guest speakers will present on related topics in music production, sound design and composition. Students will design and execute their own digital music projects. Prerequisite: None. Open to all grades.  This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Dance 1
courses.brief_description: Dance foundations, technique, and creative expression
courses.description: Dance 1 introduces students to the principles of dance to create a foundation for technically based and kinesthetically sound movement. Students will experience a diverse scope of techniques, including modern, jazz, ballet, contemporary, and cultural dance styles. Students will explore movement concepts using space, time, and energy that will eventually lead to performance. Students will have a broad range of opportunities to develop their appreciation for dance as an art form through historical, cultural, and social contexts. Prerequisite: None   This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Dance 2
courses.brief_description: Expanding technique, choreography, and creative movement
courses.description: Building on the foundational movement and choreography skills developed in Dance 1, Dance 2 is designed to expand students' movement vocabulary and further activate their creative voice.  Students will begin to develop their own creative process and movement preferences.  They will be introduced to concepts of choreography and composition through the works of traditional and contemporary  choreographers.  Students will explore movement concepts using space, time and energy that will eventually lead to performance.  They will have a broad range of opportunities to develop their appreciation for dance as an artform through historical, cultural and social contexts through unique experiences and cultivated collaborative inquiry. Prerequisite: Dance 1 This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Dance Ensemble PPP
courses.brief_description: Advanced dance technique, creativity, and service
courses.description: This class provides students with continued development and practice in the principles of technique and movement through diverse genres and styles of dance. Students will experiment with choreographic premises and apply them to their own movement preferences. This course further develops the technical foundation in all dance genres and encourages students to create and innovate their own original work. Students will continue to establish their creative process from start to stage, including dance production and dance on film. Students will have opportunities to collaborate and work with guest teachers, choreographers, and students in a variety of electives. This course builds upon the foundation established in Dance 1 and Dance 2, as students expand their depth of knowledge of dance as an art form with a continued appreciation for historical, cultural, and social contexts in their everyday lives. The PPP component includes continued work with our partnership organization. This will include raising funds and collecting items through dance performances, volunteering at organization events, and creating outreach opportunities in collaboration with different community populations.  Prerequisite: Dance 1 and Dance 2 This yearlong course is UC approved and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.

courses.title: Biology
courses.brief_description: The study of life, from the molecular level to entire ecosystems
courses.description: Biology explores life at every level, from molecules to entire ecosystems. This survey course emphasizes the unifying themes of evolution and the interconnectedness of life. Students actively examine the moral and social implications of scientific issues while engaging with topics such as ecology, evolution, genetics, and reproduction. The course highlights social and environmental justice, fostering inquiry and interpretation. Concepts come to life through laboratory experiments, simulations, discussions, and collaborative projects. Questions, examples, analogies, and real-world applications reinforce learning throughout the course. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.

courses.title: Chemistry
courses.brief_description: An exploration of the properties and transformations of matter
courses.description: In Chemistry, students explore the properties and transformations of matter. Through frequent demonstrations, laboratory experiments, interactive group discussions, and collaboration with peers, students learn the principles that underlie chemical change and learn to cultivate an attitude of inquiry about the chemical phenomena they experience in the world around them. Emphasis is placed on developing the skills necessary to design and conduct meaningful scientific investigations, interpret data, and clearly communicate the results. Students’ learning over the year culminates in a collaborative student-designed research project in which they learn to identify credible scientific sources in the media and create laboratory experiments that explore a topic connected to the well-being of our planet and its inhabitants. The process and results of students’ projects are shared and celebrated during a community-wide symposium held in May, and students reflect on the ways in which they can leverage their scientific literacy for positive change.   Prerequisite: One year of high school (9th grade) science. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: One year of high school (9th grade) science.

courses.title: Ethics in the Sciences and Technology
courses.brief_description: Moral questions that come up in the sciences and technology
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course will begin with an introduction to philosophy and great thinkers throughout history. We will then focus on ethics, particularly the thorny moral questions that come up in the sciences and technology—How can we allocate scarce organs to those waiting on a transplant list in a ‘fair’ way? Should it be allowable to ‘design’ many of the traits of a baby? Are the risks of a driverless car morally acceptable, and if so, how should driverless cars be programmed in an imminent crash? Should the atomic bomb have been made- and are there limits on using science to make weapons or other products that can cause harm? The course will invite introspection and a solution-oriented mindset. We will be learning some psychology about ourselves and our moral development, our implicit ways of figuring out right and wrong. We will evaluate what ethical systems we might reject, and what we might create in their place. How might our life experiences, debates, and discussions with our peers compel us to question our own beliefs? In the process, we will build skills in reasoning, speaking persuasively, and listening with an open, flexible mind in order to engage constructively around life’s biggest questions. Essential Questions: Just because we have the scientific ability to do something, does that always mean we should? How can examining our ethical thinking help us to lead lives of consequence and fulfillment? Prerequisites: Open to juniors and seniors.  This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Honors Biology: Behavioral Genetics and Anthropology
courses.brief_description: Genetic components that contribute to human evolution and behavior
courses.description: Behavioral Genetics and Anthropology is a yearlong honors biological anthropology lab course that focuses on the connection between evolutionary biology, genetics, and the wide range of traits influenced by gene-culture interactions in humans. We start with an introductory unit in anthropological methodology and evolutionary theory. We consider genes as a unit of natural selection and investigate genetic components contributing to human evolution and behavior.    We will explore the study of human behaviors, including but not limited to:  Compassion, competition, collaboration, altruism Gene culture coevolution  Sex and reproduction, sociosexual behavior Individual and collective violence  Symbolic behavior  Tools and technology  We will also look at the recent analysis of the human genome and genetic components that connect to complex human behaviors that impact modern culture and society. This is an interdisciplinary lab science course, meaning each unit will have a lab and/or fieldwork component. Projects will include hands-on, 3D anatomical replicas, conducting interviews and field work, and independent research on a specific human trait with a culminating final presentation. A question we will consider throughout this course is, “What, if anything, makes humans unique?” Note: May be taken in conjunction with Molecular Genetics.   Prerequisite: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science. This is a yearlong course and is UC aproved.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science.

courses.title: Honors Biology: Marine Ecology: Field and Lab Science PPP
courses.brief_description: Appreciation, preservation, and protection of marine habitats
courses.description: The world's oceans cover over 70% of the Earth's surface and are integrally tied to the health of the planet. A deep understanding of marine ecology is critical for the appreciation, preservation, and protection of marine habitats. Marine Ecology is a yearlong advanced interdisciplinary science course that uses the Bay Area as a classroom. The course will include required field trips during non-school hours. Students will be expected to meet at various locations in the Bay Area for our fieldwork and field trips (rain or shine)—planning and organization are essential skills for those taking this course. Students should expect to attend 1-2 field trips per month. Over the course of the year, students will grow to understand the physical and chemical characteristics of marine ecological zones and investigate the anatomy, behavior, and evolutionary adaptations of a variety of life. Students will investigate a broad range of current conservation concerns with an emphasis on climate change and science communication. Laboratory activities include dissection, live organism exploration, data collection, guest lectures, and microscope work. Field experiences include gathering data at the beach and intertidal zone for several community/citizen science projects, teaching elementary students, coastal cleanup day, murals exploration, seafood processing facility, and more depending on availability each year. Public purpose is woven into the curriculum of this course through collecting baseline data, science communication and outreach, public events, and learning about the thoughtful work of those in the community.  Prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science.  Students interested in Marine Ecology must complete this interest form. This UC approved course is offered yearlong and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science.

courses.title: Honors Biology: Molecular Genetics
courses.brief_description: The core concepts of molecular biology and common biotechnology techniques
courses.description: This course allows students to engage in meaningful, hands-on laboratory experiences while exploring the core concepts of molecular biology and common biotechnology techniques. Through inquiry-based learning, labs, and student-directed projects, students will develop a deep understanding of the central dogma of biology by studying DNA, RNA, proteins, and the methods scientists use to investigate molecular biology. Students will gain practical experience with essential lab techniques, including gel electrophoresis, PCR DNA amplification, PAGE, protein chromatography, and CRISPR. Additionally, they will explore the role of epigenetics in gene expression and analyze the ethical implications of genetic technology in medicine and the biotech industry. A strong emphasis will be placed on responsible academic research practices, data analysis, and the integration of mathematical skills to interpret experimental results. Throughout the course, students will be challenged to think critically about modern scientific advancements and their societal impact. Students will participate in ongoing lab work that requires attention to detail, problem-solving, and collaboration. This course is designed for a broad range of students, whether they are considering a future in science or simply have a curiosity about biology at the cellular and molecular level. Prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science.

courses.title: Honors Biology: Neuroscience and Psychology: Brain and Behavior
courses.brief_description: Exploring human behavior, mind, and development
courses.description: Using multiple perspectives, students will look at human behavior from the biological, cognitive, behavioral, psychodynamic, humanistic, social, and sociocultural points of view. An emphasis is put on how the physical brain, the environment, and human behavior continually interact and influence each other. Students examine readings and research on learning, social interactions, memory, thinking, psychological disorders, and cognitive development. Genetic and environmental factors underlying development and attachment are also considered.The hands-on portion of the course will include exploration of the human brain, neuroscience activities; social and developmental psychology observational labs; stress physiology experiments and more.   The course is an invitation for introspection and expression as students agree, disagree, and take what is helpful to them and make it their own. There is an emphasis on multiple ways of engaging with the material. Individual projects provide the opportunity for students to explore topics of their choice in more depth. Prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science. This course is offered yearlong and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science.

courses.title: Honors Biology: Science Research Fly Sci PPP
courses.brief_description: Genetic research, molecular biology techniques, model organisms
courses.description: This year-long, hands-on research course offers students the opportunity to contribute to real-world biomedical research in collaboration with Stanford University. Using Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) as a model organism, students will explore genetic research, molecular biology techniques, and the role of model organisms in biomedical science. Students will learn to maintain, characterize, and cross fruit fly strains. Students will also apply essential molecular biology techniques, including DNA extraction, PCR, and gel electrophoresis, to analyze genetic modifications.  The goal of this course is to create a genetically unique fly line using the StanX P-element, SX4. If successfully created, these genetically unique flies will be incorporated into a research repository, providing valuable resources for scientists studying diseases. Students will have the opportunity to present their work at an annual conference at Stanford and may even contribute to a peer-reviewed scientific publication. This course is ideal for students with a strong interest in biology, genetics, and research. This course is designed to be a PPP course, as we will be collaborating with Stanford and potentially establishing a stable line of flies to be used for public research, which will be housed at the University of Indiana in Bloomington. Students will be required to attend a spring conference at Stanford to share their findings. Additionally, due to the nature of this class and the upkeep of living organisms, there will be additional requirements to come in on “non-class” days to successfully maintain, characterize, and cross flies.  Prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science. Highly recommend that you have a B+ (or higher) grades from both biology and chemistry. Attendance at a Spring 2026 pre-meeting during tutorial on Monday, April 20th 2026, with Ms. Wilkinson, will be mandatory if you are considering this course. This course is offered yearlong and fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors. UC approval is pending.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science. Highly recommend that you have a B+ (or higher) grades from both biology and chemistry.

courses.title: Honors Chemistry
courses.brief_description: An investigation of the properties of acid/base, electrochemical, precipitate, and equilibrium reactions
courses.description: Chemistry Honors expands on the foundational knowledge developed in the 10th grade chemistry course by investigating the properties of acid/base, electrochemical, precipitate, and equilibrium reactions. Students will examine these reactions from both a qualitative and quantitative perspective, including the kinetics and thermodynamics of their behaviors. Emphasis is placed on understanding how bonding and molecular architecture affect chemical properties, conducting rigorous experimental analysis, and synthesizing skills from all areas of the course to address complex problems. Through frequent exploration of the connections between class material, current research, and societal challenges, students also develop proficiency in applying their knowledge to better understand the pressing issues and promises of our time. Prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science. This is a yearlong course and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of high school (9th and 10th grade) science.

courses.title: Teaching Assistant
courses.description: Juniors and seniors may serve as a Teaching Assistant (TA) in a class that they have previously taken with success. In most cases, TA’s are assigned to a specific class section, are expected to attend all class meetings, and are included in the class roll. Additionally, they should meet once a rotation outside of class with their supervising faculty member. Alternatively, in the case of science, TA’s who assist with lab preparation may meet regularly with a faculty member during a shared free block. All TA’s receive academic credit, and therefore their work should not be restricted to such tasks as photocopying and filing. Rather, they should be exposed to what it means to be a teacher through meaningful activities, such as lesson planning, testing labs, and creating evaluations; in other words, it is expected that all TA’s will have the opportunity to teach. Additionally, all TA’s are expected to produce a thoughtful reflection of their work (e.g. a portfolio, writeup of a new lab design, or conference presentation). Students may hold only one TA position per semester, and it will count as a seventh course, but not as one of a student’s six required courses. Teachers may have only one TA per class, and all TA’s are graded pass/fail. Prerequisite: TA's must have taken the course for which they will serve.
courses.prerequisites: TA's must have taken the course for which they will serve.

courses.title: Teaching Assistant Tech Arts PPP
courses.description: This course will have students apply the combined skills learned in previous Technical Arts classes with new skills focused on leadership. The faculty member will act as a mentor and coach, introducing material so that the student leader can better understand cultural competency, equitable pedagogical practices, and their impact on the learning environment. These learning strategies will then be applied and focus on four main areas on a daily basis—teaching, community, machine maintenance/class prep, and reflection. Note: This class does not fulfill the technical arts graduation requirement and PPP credit can only be given for participation Private Skills for a Public Purpose class. Prerequisites: Design & Technology along with one semester of the class for which you will be the teaching assistant. This semester long course offered in both Fall 2021 and Spring 2022 fulfills the Public Purpose Program requirement for juniors and seniors.
courses.prerequisites: Design & Technology along with one semester of the class for which you will be the teaching assistant.

courses.title: Teaching Assistantship Tech Arts
courses.description: Tech Arts teaching assistants play a vital role in helping us produce better projects and a safer environment. This is a leadership role in which you will have to share what you know, learn more about the processes you are assisting with, and seek the most effective ways to support current student projects and classroom learning. It’s a challenging, rewarding, and essential role in the Tech Arts. To become a Teaching Assistant, you must 1.have completed Design and Technology and two other shop classes. 2.In those classes, you should have shown proficiency and a commitment to safe working practices in the shops. 3.check with the instructor verbally or electronically before moving forward in the process. 4.create a written proposal outlining how you hope to be helpful in the classroom and what you hope to learn from the experience. The TA form is signed by the teacher, the department chair, and the participating instructor. Form submission is to the scheduler during course signups. No more than two students can TA per Technical Arts section. This class does not count toward your Technical Art graduation requirement and is graded as pass/fail. Prerequisite: Design & Technology and two other shop classes. This course is offered both in Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Design & Technology and two other shop classes.

courses.title: 3D-Printing and Parametric Design
courses.brief_description: The dynamic realm of parametric design
courses.description: This hands-on course introduces students to parametric design and how it connects to 3D printing and CNC machines. Students learn to use Grasshopper, a parametric design tool, to create flexible, customizable designs that can be digitally modeled and then physically built. Throughout the course, students work with a range of materials—such as wood, plastic, and metal—to bring their ideas to life. Projects may include items like holders, jewelry, or modular components, giving students a hands-on way to explore how parametric design shapes both appearance and functionality. In addition to making, students explore how digital fabrication is changing the design world and shaping future careers. By blending creativity, technology, and problem-solving, this course prepares students to confidently work with modern tools and techniques used in today’s design and fabrication industries. This class meets the Tech Arts "Design & Engineering" category requirement. Prerequisite: Design & Technology This course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Circuits and Electronics: Analog and Digital
courses.brief_description: Circuit design and assembly
courses.description: This class jumps in where the Design and Technology class left off, starting with building basic circuits and moving into designing your own custom printed circuit boards. Whether or not you think of yourself as an aspiring electrical engineer, this course will invite you to work collaboratively to learn electronics, followed by some guided design time to develop a head-turning design that will make your amplifier circuit look and sound amazing. But we don't stop there; we also jump into some microcontroller programming so you can add some digital features to your project, like music-reactive lights, a local sensor, or a live data display. What You'll Learn: Basics of circuit design and assembly. Custom printed circuit board (PCB) design. Create a functional set of Bluetooth speakers with an eye-catching design. Microcontroller programming for digital features like music-reactive lights. Project management and collaborative design techniques. Develop skills in technical problem-solving and resourcefulness. Study inclusive and sustainable electronic innovations. All skill and interest levels are welcome as class culture goals seek to break cycles of technical-skill exclusivity and product-over-purpose and elevate diverse identifiers. This class meets the "Design & Engineering" Tech Arts category requirement.  Prerequisite: Design and Technology This course is offered in Fall 2026 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Circuits and Electronics: Device Invention
courses.brief_description: Explore the dual nature of technology in our world
courses.description: What are the core elements of designing and inventing with electronics? This course invites you to become a designer and creator of connected, data-driven devices. As “inventors,” we will seek to create useful and magical electronic interfaces. What You'll Learn: Design and build IoT (Internet of Things) devices using microprocessors and single-board computers (Raspberry Pi). Engage in open-ended, collaborative projects to develop devices to improve the world. Balance refined craftsmanship with rapid prototyping techniques. Gain skills in circuitry, mechanics, coding, and creating enclosures for various electronic objects. Collaborate with peers in a flexible learning environment, guided by an instructor who facilitates and learns alongside you. Access various resources, including online documentation, peer knowledge, generative AI, and instructor support. Join in a journey of invention. All skill and interest levels are welcome, as class culture goals seek to break cycles of technical-skill exclusivity and product-over-purpose, and to elevate diverse identifiers. This class meets the Tech Arts "Design & Engineering" category requirement. Prerequisite: Design and Technology This course is offered in Spring 2027 and is UC approved.

courses.title: Code for Sound
courses.brief_description: Core concepts of data structures, algorithms, and data wrangling
courses.description: This course introduces core concepts of data structures, algorithms, and data wrangling to students already familiar with computer programming basics (syntax, debugging, control flow, functions, scope, and classes) by applying object-oriented computer programming to creative projects in digital music production. No prior experience playing or writing music is required. This class meets the Tech Arts “Design & Engineering” category requirement. Prerequisite: Design & Technology and 1) Device Invention, 2) Graphics and Game Design, or 3) equivalent prior experience. Students with prior experience from outside Tech Arts will be asked to demonstrate these skills through a code sample before enrolling; no prior experience playing or writing music is required. This semester long course is offered in both Fall 2026 and Spring 2027 and is UC approved.
courses.prerequisites: Design & Technology and 1) Device Invention, 2) Graphics and Game Design, or 3) equivalent prior experience. Students with prior experience from outside Tech Arts will be asked to demonstrate these skills through a code sample before enrolling; no prior experience playing or writing music is required.

courses.title: Design & Technology
courses.brief_description: The many facets of design and the infinite possibilities of object making
courses.description: This course explores the many facets of design and the infinite possibilities of object making. Creative problem solving through exploration in design principles and hands-on prototyping serves as the groundwork for advancement in later Technical Arts courses. This cross-disciplinary course emphasizes skill-building, collaboration, critical thinking, and project management.
